utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, I'd like to go back over what we had agreed on with regard to the interview, and then I would like to move on to the key event. You said that from the 20th of May until the 19th of November, 1992, you were outside of Bratunac, and you can't talk about that, or those events, because you have no direct information about such events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have said is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that 56 to 58 soldiers from your brigade were killed after Srebrenica had been declared to be a demilitarised zone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. About -- well, not about, but I had a list with the exact number from the time that Srebrenica was declared a demilitarised zone and up to the time of the fall of Srebrenica, between 56 and 58 soldiers were killed, and I have already told you about the exact list of those killed. I said that Mr. Ivanisevic has that precise list, in fact, because he took charge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that institution for investigations -- or you provided that institute for investigations a lot of information about villages that had been torched and about the wartime events; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning all the information I obtained while I was in Bratunac, with the exception of the period that you have just mentioned, I provided all the information I had which was in written form. I provided all that information either to that institute or to a different department. I don't know the exact name. They worked in Bijeljina. There were three or four individuals who worked on the documentation of war crimes. Amongst other things, they gathered information on villages that had been torched, about buildings that had been destroyed and so on and so forth. I provided them with such information. I think they worked within the framework of the MUP, but I don't know the exact name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also told us that you never considered the DutchBat to be your -- or, rather, our enemy, and you did not believe that at one point in time they would join the Muslims in the course of some conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that those were my exact words. I did say -- in fact, I assume -- or, rather, I don't assume. I know that we spoke about the Dutch Battalion and my attitude to DutchBat. Naturally I didn't consider them to be enemies, but I also said the following, I would like to add this, I said the following: DutchBat members, in my assessment -- well, I analysed them in the following manner: If there were to be a conflict according to my intelligence and counter-intelligence assessments, I had several options. The first one was that DutchBat would remain neutral if there were a Muslim-Serb clash. The second option was that DutchBat - and this is the worst case scenario - the second option would be that DutchBat would join up with the Muslim forces and would confront the Serbian forces. And the third option which I always considered to be possible was that at one point in time DutchBat might not accept to be engaged together with the Muslims and given the strength and so on and so forth, the Muslims might quite simply try to force them to act with the Muslims against the Serb side, or they would try and seize their equipment and weapons and use that against the Serbs. So those were the options I had in my intelligence and counter-intelligence assessments. These are the options that I assumed to be possible, but I do apologise, Mr. Karadzic, it is true that I never considered them to be enemies, and I didn't think they had such an attitude towards us. That was never my opinion. I apologise for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine but were any one -- was anyone held as a hostage for a few days? Given the options that you mentioned, were there any indications that they could be threatened by the 28th Division. In the Bandera Triangle, for instance. In the Bandera Triangle were there any such indications?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the incident that you have mentioned. DutchBat officers confirmed this to me. I heard what happened in the Suceska sector where Zulfo Tursunovic was the brigade commander. Officers confirmed that Zulfo Tursunovic, together with his forces attacked them, disarmed them, and held them as hostages for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that at the beginning of the event in July 1995, on the 10th or 11th, they shot at and killed a Dutch soldier at the Echo Observation Post in the direction of Zeleni Jadar?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I obtained that information from DutchBat members. The soldier who was killed was evacuated via the Yellow Bridge, so I do know about the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we are discussing this, it is not from the interview, but nevertheless is it correct that some of them moved over to our side and you -- or, rather, our troops provide them with accommodation in the Fontana Hotel in Bratunac -- or, rather, where did you find accommodation for them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. About 30 soldiers and officers, together with APCs and equipment, moved over to the Serbian side, and at the beginning, they were in Hotel Fontana, and then they had accommodation in the Djuro Pucar secondary school building, the new building that was open at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You confirmed that you never said, you never testified, that I knew about the events in July 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd ask Mr. Karadzic to think about that question and perhaps rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is not clear. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have a look to see how it was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson asked whether he knew that I knew or did not know about the events in July 1995, and Mr. Nikolic said that he had never made such a claim. What is your position about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. Robinson asked me the question, I know exactly what he asked me given the way it was interpreted. He asked me whether I had any information according to which Mr. Karadzic knew that the prisoners from Bratunac would be killed that evening on the 13th -- or, rather, on the evening between the 12th and 13th. I said that I did not know what Mr. Karadzic knew about that, because I quite simply didn't have any link with Mr. Karadzic. I said that I had never testified about what you knew at that time, on that day, that evening. All I said is that I testified that Miroslav Deronjic, in relation to the fate of the prisoners, referred to instructions that he had received from the president of the republic, from Mr. Karadzic, instructions that he had received in relation to the fact that the prisoners had to go from Bratunac, and Miroslav Deronjic said that he did not want those prisoners to be killed in Bratunac. He said that he had enough problems as it was and that they had to leave the territory of the municipality of Bratunac. That is what I told Mr. Robinson. So I want to be quite clear. I don't know what you knew on the 12th or the 13th because I never had any contact with you. I had no information about the information that you had at your disposal. I only referred to what Mr. Miroslav Deronjic himself said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on that occasion you mentioned the possibility, I didn't even ask you about this, that perhaps my name had been taken advantage of by him or others. Perhaps they would say that they had spoken to Karadzic about some things and so on and so forth. Sometimes people would invoke my name, but perhaps that wasn't the case. It was an abuse, perhaps, of my name. Did he abuse my name, or did someone else do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, I am going to put on the record that that question -- that Mr. Nikolic did not say that in the interview, that the name had been taken in vain many times, according to my notes and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Instead of referring that interview, why don't you put the question directly to the witness now, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there the possibility that people might abuse my name and say that they were close to me or that they had contact with me or that I told them something?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be very explicit in my answer and tell you whether someone used your name for purposes of manipulation. I can't say anything about that, but what I can confirm is that very frequently Miroslav Deronjic, Ljubisa Simic, members of the civilian authorities, and Miroslav Deronjic in particular, often invoked your name. As to whether that was a case of abuse, as to whether you really said all these things to him, suggested all these things to him, the things that he referred to, well, I don't know. But he often invoked your name, said something to the effect of you having made such and such an order, taken such and such a decision, but whether that was a case of abuse or whether that was the truth, whether he really had contact with you or not, I really can't say because I wasn't that close to Miroslav Deronjic, and I'd never met you. I'd never seen you personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the interview you also said when we asked you how it was that the people were killed, you said -- or you mentioned as the main reason that there was a lot of hatred, pathological hatred, in fact long-lasting hatred, and you said that that was the main reason; is that correct? Not a justification, but it was an explanation of the way in which these things occurred?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned some of the things that I said. I was a little more precise. I said that with regard to all the events that unfolded down there, there was absolutely no justification. There are no reasons, or, in fact, there's nothing that could be justified. I apologise. There are no reasons that can justify that crime. I quite clearly said, and I'm only expressing my own opinion, I said that there was a historical context, historical background to those conflicts in Podrinje and the area where I live. I said -- well, I think I mentioned the Second World War and various crimes and killings that occurred in the area, and both sides committed murder on a mass scale in the previous wars. I also said this these events, these crimes, these cases of murders hadn't been forgotten in spite of the fact that 50 years had passed. They had not been forgotten. I further said that the very course of the war, the conflict from 1992 to 1995, well, it was a very bloody affair on both sides, and then I also said that from 1992 up until 1995 in that area, in the area of Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Konjevic Polje, Vlasenica, and in Zepa, I said that they destroyed -- both sides destroyed everything they could. They looted property, torched property. And this would pass from one person to another. The Serbs would loot the areas -- the Muslim areas, and then the Muslims would take this back and loot the Serbian people. They'd take everything they could find. And in the course of those operations, in the course of those fights, a lot of terrible crimes were committed. There were a lot of victims. And I spoke about the pathological hatred that prevailed in that area right up until 1995. So that was my explanation with regard to the reasons, the possible motives, for the conflict and for the crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And as for these various actions and this mutual destruction, no order was needed from anyone. This happened according to some centuries-long automatic reflex. Am I right when I say that, on the basis of terrible experience from the previous wars?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I would like you to be precise in putting questions. What do you mean by this, "this happened according to some centuries long automatic reflex," no orders necessary, what is this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, did I say that actually? Was it interpreted correctly? I said automatism. I didn't say "reflex." But anyway, I'm asking whether it was indispensable for this to be planned, to have planned actions, or were they simply killing each other? One village was killing another given any opportunity during the course of the war. So the Serbs from your area of responsibility, did they wait for some order from you to fight, or the Muslims on the other side, or was it, as you explained it, according to a dictat of hate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, it's a compound question, and it's confusing fighting and killing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So the answer may not be clear unless it's broken down. Because he started talking about killings, and it wasn't clear what exact period we were talking about, and now he's talking about fighting without an order, if it was translated correctly. So I think it needs to be made simpler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I do apologise. I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can it be put this way: That things happened -- actually, that in this war, one did not have to issue orders to the effect of "fire." Rather, the order that had to be issued was stop this willingness to have a conflict, to take revenge, to kill. It was not always guided but was born of chaos. That's my question. Did some village from your area of responsibility wait for an order to fight, or if it is attacked, did they fight and would they go after each other? What I'm trying to say is: Was this a controlled process or did it evolve according to the laws of chaos?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood your first question, too, and it was absolutely clear to me what it was that you were asking, so I can answer you and I will. You put part of that question to me during the interview as well, and in that context I am going to answer this question as well. In order to carry out an operation, I absolutely rule out what you said. I mean, I rule out planning, organisation, and particularly what you referred to, that there was no command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not talking about 1995. I'm talking about the history of conflict, about attacks of one village against another and so on. For example, was that always planned or were these sudden attacks, sudden conflicts? I'm not talking about July 1995. I'm talking about the many torchings of villages and looting and killings.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever period you speak about, any period, when speaking about military operations, I mean, I am just talking about military operations. So when talking about military operations, in my view as a soldier, as an officer, I have to say that the element of command and control cannot be excluded, meaning to say that if you want to attack someone, if you are to attack a village or anything that you believe is a target for a military attack, you have to plan that. At least that's the way I operated. So in my unit, always, wherever I was, if you plan something as a military operation, you have to plan it beforehand. Then you have to organise, prepare that action, and you have to carry it out. In order to carry it out, you have to command. So all of these are elements that are indispensable in order to start an operation. In the operation itself, in that part, that is so say, after you had planned it, organised it, prepared it, ordered what was supposed to be done, so now during that part of the operation, as the operation is underway, there are some things that you cannot keep under your control. I explained that to you during the interview as well. And that is the moment that you asked me about, and that is revenge, killings, murders based on revenge. I told you then and I'm telling you now that these were individual acts, individual crimes. They did happen, and they are part of an armed conflict. They are part of any struggle. I spoke about that to you when we had the interview, and that was my understanding of your question as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have explained that now fully, and that also has to do with the part when you said that the Serbs fled from Srebrenica to Bratunac and the Muslims from Bratunac to Srebrenica, that all the villages where the fighting was taking place had been torched and that everything had been destroyed. So as for this nonmilitary part, you say that that had not been ordered. Rather, it was the way that you had put it. So this nonmilitary or unsoldierly behaviour was part of that revenge or that wish to take revenge.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. Obviously the transcript's not done yet. I spoke about revenge as part of a military operation. So within a military operation, a military operation, an attack. You also have an individual act of revenge. These are individual crimes that are committed, but they are committed within the attack. They do not take place separately. In specific situations -- or, rather, we had situations when individual crimes were committed out of revenge and there weren't any operations underway. There weren't any combat operations underway, but I'm talking about crimes that were committed during the course of attacks or active military operations on both sides. So I'm not making any distinction there and there wasn't a distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us conclude on that topic. Can we say that we had the misfortune of all of these wars with the participation of a foreign factor also included a component of a civil war? That is to say that neighbours of different faiths and ethnic backgrounds fought during those wars with foreign powers, the First World War victims on that account, the Second World War, and so on. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I agree. That is the historical context in which all wars were waged, all wars that I know of, in the territory of the former Yugoslavia and beforehand, before Yugoslavia as such was established. So that is the historical context that went on, especially the Second World War. The war that took place after that, in essence, there was a conflict based on inter-ethnic hatred and differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like us to shed some light on the very beginning of the operation and the operation itself. Is it correct that the operation started as a legitimate operation of separating the enclaves and reducing the Srebrenica enclave to its agreed borders even if there was disagreement concerning those boundaries? So I'm referring to the operation itself, when you felt that it would be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about the intention of the Army of Republika Srpska in view of the attack against the Srebrenica enclave, I've explained that before, and of course I'm going to explain it now as well. The first intention of the Army of Republika Srpska was to separate, physically separate, the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa and to free the road that led to Milici and the road that led to Skelani. Since this is viva voce testimony, I said last time I testified, and I would like to repeat that fact once again, in my view -- it is my conviction, rather, that the attack against Srebrenica started approximately on the day when the observation point at Zeleni Jadar was taken by the Serb forces. For me, roughly that would be the date when the preparatory part started for bringing in equipment and forces from the area of Zeleni Jadar, from the southern part, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember whether that was the 9th, 10th, or 11th? Can you remember the date? It was the 10th, wasn't it? The 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack against the observation point in Zeleni Jadar occurred on the 31st of May, and roughly until this check-point was taken until units were organised in that area, this went on, say, until the 30th, 31st of May. Actually, the 5th of June. So it was almost a month before the attack against Srebrenica, so the attack from that area, Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. But what happened when this Dutch soldier was killed, when the Dutch left Echo, what date was that? Do you remember? That was the 9th, 10th or 11th. No, it wasn't the 11th. 9th or 10th of July; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour -- sorry to interrupt. We're talking about day when Private Renssen was killed. I think it's well established. It's not, I think, in dispute, and I think Mr. Karadzic should be able to put the correct date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And to be clear, where was it? I don't think you would dispute that Private Renssen was killed by Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When was it, to be clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It as 8 July, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 8 July. Where was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have to check which OP it was near, Your Honour. I don't want to say -- I know but I need to -- I want to make sure I get it right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But with all due respect for the learned Mr. Nicholls, I'm interested in what this witness knows, not in hearing what I know or what Mr. Nicholls knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, I know that. And I'm sorry, but I need to respond to that. It's okay to cross-examine and of course it's okay to test the witness's knowledge and recollection, but it's not okay to put forward dates or incidents which are known to be incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, do you follow, Mr. Karadzic? You said, 9th, 10th, 11th. That's why Mr. Nicholls intervened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for that. I wanted to be of assistance. I wanted to help the witness to remember as soon as he could. 1D5080, could we have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know of this order of the 2nd Corps ordering the 28th Division to prepare for offensive operations aimed at liberating the territory of BiH, inflicting losses upon the aggressor forces, I think, and so on. The 17th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do have a translation, but I don't think it has been uploaded yet, so can we place the translation on the ELMO, and can we keep the Serbian version in e-court and then we'll upload the translation later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please zoom in so that I can see the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just while that's coming up, it was OP Foxtrot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask the witness whether as an intelligence officer he was aware of this order that had to do with preparations, and did he notice the preparations carried out by the 28th Division for offensive operations that would be in line with this order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I can find my bearings here. When can I start? Mr. Karadzic, this is the first time I've seen this document. Preparations to launch an attack, an order to the command of the 28th Division, this is the first time I've seen it. Yesterday, I told you that my intelligence assessments and also what I reported to my superior command contained the following information: I believed -- or, rather, I had information according to which an attack by the 28th Division forces was being prepared jointly with units of the ABiH 2nd Corps, which would set out from the Tuzla sector, and units of the 28th Division and a brigade from Zepa would set out from Srebrenica. They would join up somewhere in the Sekovici-Crni Vrh sector. Those were my assessments, but I had no information according to which there was a written order or any other kind of order that related to an attack of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be the next Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2079, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now see 22818, which is a 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an extraordinary combat report from the Drina Corps command, the forward command post Pribicevac, dated the 9th of July. Please have a look at it. We can also have a look at the translation. It is sending this from Pribicevac to the Main Staff and command of the Drina Corps. Do you agree? And it says -- or, rather, it describes what the enemy defended. Further down it says that the enclaves were separated on the 9th of July. They carried out a task and created the conditions to continue with the attack in the direction of Srebrenica. And then in the third part it says attack in the direction of Srebrenica. So you still can't see that there's a decision to enter Srebrenica itself, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we should have a translation for this. Where is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's been uploaded. There should be a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we have it. Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Attack towards Srebrenica. It's been correctly translated. So on the 9th there was no order to enter Srebrenica, but to continue in the direction of Srebrenica. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this interim report, I can't fail to notice item 2. This interim report is one I haven't previously seen, but very rapidly, on the 9th of July, 1995, our units carried out a fierce attack along the axis of Zeleni Jadar-Srebrenica-Pribojevici village, Podravanje village and Kvarac -- I apologise, Kvarac, Srebrenica, and reached the Divljakinje-Olovine trig point 684, Zivkovo Brdo and so on. In your question you said that an immediate task had been carried out on the basis of this document. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this part here, I'm reading through item 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the margin, because you can't see that part. Below Alibegovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And thus they separated the Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves and carried out this immediate task.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to talk about. Yes. The factual situation that is mentioned in this interim report of the 9th of July, well, I'm a hundred per cent sure about this. The separation of the Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves were carried out on that day that the Zeleni Jadar check-point was taken in the southern part of the enclave, the Echo check-point. And those two enclaves were physically separated when this route was liberated, when the Zeleni Jadar-Milici route was liberated and the Zeleni Jadar-Skelani route was liberated, then those two enclaves were also physically separated. Taking the positions in the Zeleni Jadar sector and controlling that part, those roads, resulted in such a separation. I'm saying this so that we could be able to go into the details in an appropriate manner later. In my opinion, that was when the immediate task was implemented. The two enclaves, if we had sufficient forces, could be physically separated. We could take those parts, those positions that were physically separated. So we did have the possibility of doing that at the time. That was the factual situation, and this was before the 9th of July, 1995. As for the forces continuing to enter the enclave and going to those positions, well, that constituted an entrance into the enclave. It was no longer a matter of separating the enclave -- enclaves, it was matter of entering the depth of the enclaves. So these were attacks carried out by the VRS army along that axis Zeleni Jadar-Srebrenica, and they reached the lines of these features we have mentioned. I don't want to read through them. This is just to provide you with a clarification as to when this immediate task was carried out. It was far earlier than what was is stated in this combat report.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked not to speak so close to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this please be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be Exhibit D2080.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you seen a telegram in which General Tolimir informed the forward command post that he had informed me that this was successful and he asked for approval to enter Srebrenica? He said that I had told him that I had approved of this and assigned tasks to him. Have you seen this? Have you been shown that telegram dated the 9th of July? If not, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen a lot of documents. If you have that document, if you could remind me, fine, but I've seen a lot of documents, so I can't speak about any documents off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can find it, we'll have a look at -- it's been admitted into evidence. Let me ask you something else. As an officer, is it correct that in such situations it is essential to maintain combat contact with the enemy and you have to be at the enemy's heels? You mustn't let the enemy move back without following the enemy. You have to maintain combat contact with the enemy. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, whenever it is possible in military terms, the unit, the army unit that is attacking always strives to have combat contact with the enemy for very simple military reasons. When you have such contact, you can then engage your forces, direct the attack of your forces in an appropriate manner, and whenever an attack is launched - and I'm speaking from the point of view of the intelligence organ - whenever you do launch an attack, you engage units that can gather information on their preparations, on their movements, on their withdrawals, on them fleeing, and so on and so forth. So immediate combat contact with units is desirable if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that such continuous contact is possible to prevent the enemy from consolidating its forces and from launching a counter-attack?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've provided you with a number of reasons. One of the reasons is the one you have just mentioned, but there are far more reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just -- Your Honours, I think the document Mr. Karadzic was referring to that he said he might try to find, if I have it right, it's P02276 I think is the one he was thinking of, if that helps him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness please be shown that document. Well, there's the document. Could it please be enlarged. The Serbian version, could it please be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This telegram corresponds to the interim report, doesn't it? On the 9th of July, General Tolimir says that he informed me of the events -- please read through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should we show the witness first the bottom of the page so that he knows who signed the document. Then we scroll up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karadzic, when you show me documents, could you please tell me what is important so that I don't read through the entire document on each occasion. Please tell me what is important so that I can have a look at that. I don't like commenting on a document if I don't have the time to read through the entire document. And we're wasting a lot of time. I've seen this document. Roughly speaking, I know what it's about. I can see what it says, but if there is a paragraph that is important, a paragraph that I should pay particular attention to, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. We could expedite this. When you see this -- when you saw the interim combat report and now that you see this telegram from General Tolimir which says that it was on the 9th that the army considered that there were conditions to advance and the idea was, in fact, to move on, and that idea arose because there wasn't fierce resistance mounted, and there was considerable success in making our advance, and the resistance mounted was feeble and that was unexpected.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the date, well, I would say that the reporting date is the same. The date of the information from Pribicevac and the date of this information forwarded to you by Mr. Deputy Commander -- could you scroll up so that I can see? Mr. Zdravko Tolimir, assistant commander in the Main Staff for -- assistant commander for security. The conditions for continuing with the advance had been created. That was the conclusion, but I will tell you something that you probably don't know. Up until the 8th or 9th, during those first few days on the axis of engagement of our forces in the Zeleni Jadar area, there were perhaps problems with the advance, it didn't go that smoothly. There was fierce resistance at the beginning, and this is why we didn't advance or why the advance did not proceed more rapidly. From the 6th to the 8th, there were problems amongst our ranks, because the forces could not advance and they did not want to move on. So there are a number of reasons for which this date is referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any victims amongst our soldiers up until the 9th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. According to the information that I had, I think that during initial period of time, but I don't know the exact dates, I can no longer remember them, but during that initial period of time we had one or two soldiers who were killed and maybe two soldiers who were seriously wounded, something like that, and that's why the attack was halted. We had a break, consolidated our forces, and then continued with the attack. But as far as I can see, they are informing you of the 9th, of that date, when the advance was considerable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was when this initial resistance had been broken; is that correct? They reported to me once this resistance had been broken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my recollection, roughly speaking that would be the period in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in your testimony, on page 24608, lines 10 to 13 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you are leaving this document, could we collapse the English translation and zoom in in B/C/S part. Could we show the top of the page. Could we zoom into that stamp, yes. Mr. Nikolic, if you could help us reading that stamp. Does it refer to this report being received by somebody or sent out to some -- to some organ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we start at the beginning, at the top, because I can't see this very clearly. I can't read it. "ECV," "Name of organ." That's what I can decipher, "Name of organ." And then -- could you move that? I don't know what it says here. "ROV," as far as I can see. "ROV," I don't know what sort of an abbreviation that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Or REV?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: REV, I don't know what that means either. It might be evidence, wartime evidence -- I'm just guessing now. I don't know what it is, but I'm trying to help you now. I don't know. War evidence, that's what it makes me think of. That's the first thing that comes to mind. And below that it says "Delivered." Does it say "Delivered" here? "Recorded," and then it says "Number." The second word is illegible. I don't understand it. Number 365CA. On the 9th of July, 1995, 2350, which is probably the time. The last line, I believe it says "Certified by," and then in brackets, "Signature." Then we have "TOP, TGR." I really have no idea what that stands for. That's as far as I can go in deciphering this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does this 365 number, 36525, refer to military post? So can you tell us what organ that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My association when I look at that is that it might be the number of a document or a report that is being sent. I think that military post numbers had at least four digits, as far as I recall. This reminds me, rather, of the number of a document that was registered or logged in a book or a ledger. That's the only thing that comes to mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you read the signature part, as far as you can read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said a moment ago that it seemed to say "certified," but now I see that the word is "processed" or "registered." And the signature is the signature of a person who processed the document, but I am unfamiliar with the signature itself. I have no idea who it could be. I don't know the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. This tells that this was received at 11.50 at night.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If we look at the part "Delivered," and then in the next line we have the date, which is the 9th of July, the year 1995, at 2350, which would mean that the report was delivered at 11.50 p.m. that day, the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you upload the previous document, Exhibit D2080, which we saw earlier on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I can assist with two things. Could the words you can't read be "Order number 365"? It seems to me that way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you can take up after my question is over. Shall we see D2080. Yes. Why don't we zoom in to the stamp. Could you help us read this part again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The first word is "Received." Then in the same line we have day and month, which is the 9th of July. Next we have hour and minutes, which is 2320. So 11.20 p.m. And then signature. Of the person who received it. In the next line, "Code-name," none. So it was not a coded -- a secret document. Telegram number, 26. I don't know what the next words mean, "Br.grupa."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The English translation says "Group number." Does it ring a bell with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Group number." Yes, that seems logical. Then is this a 3? And the rest is unclear. Is it a 3 or a 9? I can't read the rest. I don't want to make a mistake. Then next we have "Urgency," zero -- or O. Then the next word is "way" or "means," and then I can't see the other word. And then last item is page number or number of pages, and then the last word is covered by a signature. In the next line we have "processed," then date and month, the month of July, hour and minute 2320, and signature, the signature the person processing it. "Delivered" is the last line, date and month, none. Hour and minute none, and signature. So it was received, processed, but not delivered. That's what I can read from the stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. But received at 11.20. The first line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Once again, this so-called group number, 300, and 365 that we saw in the earlier telegram, do they ring a bell to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then it's the same telegram number. If we have 365 on both, then it's the same telegram. That's the only link I can make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if we are to say the telegram, General Tolimir's telegram is written in response to this telegram written by General Krstic, we now know that it was responded in half an hour. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the only logic I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have a look at the top of the first page. I wanted to ask Mr. Nikolic this:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this telegram from the forward command post was sent to the Main Staff and the Drina Corps command but not to the president, and do you agree that the president did not receive documents directly from the corps but from the Main Staff, which was the way things were usually done?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say the following: It was customary, it was customary that subordinated and lower-ranking commands communicate amongst each other, and I can't address that level because I really don't know how you communicated with the Main Staff, and I don't want to speculate. In terms of technical procedure, it was possible from the forward command post to send something directly to you. Or not only you, but one can simply put "Drina Corps command, VRS Main Staff, President of the Republic," and if this is what we could see on the document, I would say you were in receipt of this, but I can't make that conclusion because we have the addressees. And when it is addressed as it was, the operator doesn't do anything otherwise. He sends it to the addressees. Based on this telegram, I cannot conclude that it was sent directly to you. Of course, I don't want to speculate. In all likelihood, in my view this telegram was sent to the Main Staff, as is stated here, and then you were informed by the Main Staff -- or my conclusion is that another telegram was drafted that was sent from the Main Staff to you. That's as far as I can guess. I would do it that way if I wanted to forward this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The previous document was admitted, and this one was admitted as well. At page 24608, you confirmed that in Srebrenica there were many legitimate military targets such as unit commands, warehouses, et cetera. I wanted to show you a document which makes reference to those legitimate military targets that were abundant in Srebrenica itself. Please bare with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You may proceed to answer, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I quoted you -- or, rather, interpreted your words at page 24608. You said: "Let us be clear again. There were legitimate military targets in Srebrenica such as commands, warehouses where war supplies were kept, equipment, and weapons. They were legitimate targets irrespective of the fact that they were inside the town." That is your position, and we agree on that, don't we?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that. Any command, any military depot, anything that in any way is made use of by the army or its commands or members of such armed forces, they are all legitimate targets no matter where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll find the document shortly. It is their document, which is an overview of their own infrastructure in the town. While we are waiting for it, I just wanted to say that you mentioned a column on the same page of the transcript. Do you remember having established that the local authorities sent out couriers to the population in general, stating that all inhabitants should go towards the UN base and that the able-bodied men should go to Jaglici and Susnjari, where they would assemble?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about their decisions, especially at the moment when Srebrenica had already fallen, basically. I only know what I observed myself, what we could see, and which is that, indeed, the civilians went to Potocari. All information we received on the 11th in the evening or at around midnight or early on the 12th, all that information we received from our neighbouring units, especially the Milici Brigade, as well as from our own units, that is to say, the 1st Infantry Battalion and the Zvornik Battalion, all that information indicated that there were many armed people assembling in the area of Jaglici and the area you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D5103. Can we have a look at that, please. Thank you. 1D5103.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document, Mr. Nikolic, did you yourself participate in that operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the operation that had to do with taking Srebrenica, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I took part in that. I was a member of the Bratunac Brigade, a unit that took part in combat operations related to Srebrenica. And within my own remit, I took part in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at this. This is their report from the 22nd of February, 1995, to the Secretariat of Defence of Tuzla that they belonged to, and now they are saying that Lovac was the commander of the 8th Operations Group in Srebrenica. Was that your information as well? And then all these other locations. As an intelligence man, did you have access to all of this and did you establish things more or less along these lines?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please give me a moment to take a look at this, because this document is one that I see for the first time again, I think. All right. Basically, I can tell you that I did know roughly -- no, not roughly, exactly. For a number of these locations I did know about that. Lovac, the staff of the Territorial Defence in Srebrenica, and so on. So all of these are locations that I was aware of before the war as well. I mean, well, it's not only before the war. I know to this day where they are, of course, especially the premises of the Territorial Defence Staff that were there when I worked and when I came to visit Srebrenica. So that was it. I also have to say for the Trial Chamber that I had a working map of the intelligence organ where I had marked the positions, the buildings where these commands were. Of course, I no longer remember all of them, but I did have this work map that remained in the safe of my office when I was demobilised. I left that as documents that could be used later as well. So my answer is in the affirmative, that many of the buildings mentioned here are buildings that I was aware of as an intelligence man.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we show the second page as well. Do you also know this professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He is a colleague of mine, Suljo Hasanovic. I know him personally. I knew him before the war, and I know exactly who he is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, have you finished with this page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be admitted on -- do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, but Mr. Reid tells me it's already in evidence as D01994. It apparently came in during Mr. Kingori's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you give the number again, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Nikolic, take a look at this. Does this also include private houses, privately owned restaurants, as well as headquarters, warehouses, well, villages are referred to as well, but this is a rather dense network of military infrastructure in Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to be clear for the Trial Chamber. Srebrenica is a tiny, tiny town that is in this valley. Whatever you wanted to have in Srebrenica, I mean, all of these commands and units that were mentioned beforehand, there were quite a few of them in a very restricted area, in a very small area. The town has a single street, this main street, and then some tiny little alleys in addition to that. And then it's about half a kilometre, 800 metres. Srebrenica itself is such that the number of these military targets, commands, is such that they only have, say, 50 metres between two of them. Lovac is the farthest away, and that's 800 metres. So it's a narrow street. Just as you said, a great many buildings in a very small area. That is how I can explain it to you as picturesquely as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you gave an interview to the commission of Republika Srpska for Srebrenica in 2004, on the 27th of September, and in that interview you said that the Bratunac Brigade never received a detailed plan for this operation concerning Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did speak to the commissioner of Republika Srpska and, among other things, we discussed that matter too. I don't know to what extent you actually quoted what I had said, but I said that the Bratunac Brigade never had a detailed plan and this is what I meant by that. Every brigade, every unit, including my brigade, the Bratunac Brigade, when such large-scale operations are involved or military operations in general, elaborates a plan of its involvement and within that plan the Bratunac Brigade wrote up all necessary combat documents. When I said that the Bratunac Brigade did not have a detailed plan, I met -- meant this detailed elaboration. So this is the procedure involved: The corps command sends you their plan of attack against Srebrenica and then on the basis of that plan you as a unit have a certain task. The Bratunac Brigade within the attack against Srebrenica had a task. So my brigade had a task. We were supposed to get together and apply regular procedure in working out all the documents that would have to do with our task within the task of the corps command. When I said that the Bratunac Brigade never had a detailed plan of attack and in the Bratunac Brigade we never worked on combat documents that had to do with the portion of our unit. All of that was done at the level of the command of the Drina Corps. My commander went there. Within the command of the Drina Corps they elaborated these combat documents and my unit was given this task. Such a procedure is soldierly and it is in accordance with the law. This kind of procedure is referred to as an abbreviated procedure, but what I was talking about was all necessary combat documents in my brigade, the Bratunac Brigade, did not elaborate all the necessary combat documents for that operation. So that is my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps this is a bit of speculation, but do you believe that this might have been the case because the plan was a rather fluid one at corps level itself. We see that there was a request to continue to the action or operation. If you don't know anything about this, you can say so. Things were fluid on their level, too, except for the immediate task of separating the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I really don't want to -- I mean, I'm a captain. I'm a reserve captain. I don't want to take it upon myself to assess the plans that were elaborated by my command of the Drina Corps. These plans were drafted by generals who are above me as far as their knowledge is concerned, so I do not give myself the right to assess what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, as they say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if it is convenient, we'll take a break now, after which you have one hour and 20 minutes, so you should wrap up your cross-examination during the next session. We will resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I will try to put questions that can be answered with a yes or no only. Is it correct that you had some knowledge then and other things you learned later, for example, concerning the participation of the army -- or, rather, the police, the MUP? You found out about that from what the OTP showed to you, and you spoke about that in the information report of the 4th of July, 2003, on page 1; right? You learned some things during these preparations and subsequently, if you will?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course. In the structure of my knowledge, there are certain things that I participated in myself, then there is knowledge that I have that is based on my investigations as a security organ, and there is also knowledge that I acquired later from documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like us to make a distinction between what you knew then and what you learned later and became convinced of later. In the Blagojevic transcript, you said that you had never seen an order about this operation and the participation of your brigade and your personal tasks. This had to do with this operation regarding Srebrenica. Blagojevic transcript, page 1989.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said when I testified then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that on the 11th there was a column towards Potocari, and then you said that in addition to indirect fire, the Serb forces around Srebrenica had opportunities to open fire directly, for example, using the B1 gun, and that the column had been targeted. However, do you agree or do you know that there weren't many casualties? There were some persons who were wounded, but there weren't many fatalities in Srebrenica during the take-over the Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the exact number of casualties was. I said that according to my information, there were casualties in the town of Srebrenica itself during the artillery fire that came from the positions of the Bratunac Brigade. And also I said that according to my information, there were civilian casualties among the people who were moving towards Bratunac, because they were directly fired at by the B1 gun that belonged to the 2nd Infantry Battalion. So these were the cases that I had information about and that I spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Testimony was heard here that another unit that had T-84. Is that correct that it was one of the best tanks at the time and that it had very good equipment and very good sights, and it could target very precisely? Are you familiar with this equipment?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I know what T-84 tanks are. Well, of course I don't know -- I mean, I'm not from that particular speciality. I am an infantryman myself, but I know basically that this is a modern tank with sights that can be used in any situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Investigator Ruez testified here, stating that they were surprised by the small number of casualties there. Is it correct that 20 or 22 persons were seriously wounded and that you took care of them, that they had been taken care of at the health centre where there was a clinic for that particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not wish to link that up, what you put as a question and the wounded who were at the clinic in Bratunac. For the Trial Chamber, there were several wounded persons who were put up at this clinic in Bratunac, more than 20-something, or the 20-something that you referred to. So on the basis of everything that I know, these two things cannot be linked up. It is possible that among those wounded who were brought to Bratunac, there were also wounded persons who had been wounded in the town of Srebrenica, even civilians who were moving, who were on the move, but I don't know the structure of the wounded. I don't know where they were wounded, how they were wounded. For me, they were only wounded persons and nothing more than that, and I don't know anything more than that, and I do not wish to speculate in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection. I am going to request cites. There was a cite to what Mr. Ruez testified to. I'm not objecting, but I would like a cite just so that I can easily find what is being referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have done that if we had time. I think Mr. Nicholls is more familiar with the case than I am. But I don't have time, so I won't refer to things that I don't have in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In order not to waste time, be precise when you refer to specify testimony. Do not paraphrase in a general term. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I would just suggest that it wastes more time when I have to stand up and ask for cites than if he just reads them out, and I don't know why he doesn't have those available when he's referring to prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But this time Mr. Nikolic clarified, but let's move on. In the future, be precise when you'd like to refer to specific part of other witness's testimony in putting your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your interview of the 28th of May, 2003, this is a report on the conversation and it's also on the Blagojevic transcript, page 1639, and it is an investigative report on the conversation with Momir Nikolic, dated the 16th of September, 2003, page 1. And there you also said -- or, in fact, you made a correction. You said that these weren't the civilians who were -- who were targeted. You said that legitimate military features were targeted. Isn't that correct? Or that they were legitimate military targets.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of details are missing in order for me to answer your question in concrete terms. I don't understand the question very well and I don't really know whom you are referring to when you say that they are legitimate military targets. Could you please clarify your question so that I could answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we call up the interview dated -- or from the year 2003. And could we see page 1 from that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just want to be precise and see what Mr. Karadzic's referring to. On page 1639 of the Blagojevic transcript, when asked about targeting, the question was: "Aside from the shelling of Srebrenica town, were you aware of any other targeting of civilians or civilian objects?" The question was: "You said that these weren't civilians who were targeted." That's at previous page 37, around line 11. The answer given by Mr. Nikolic in part was: "I know for a fact that civilians were being targeted, civilians who were on the move, and those were certainly no military units travelling down the road." Now, is that the section Mr. Karadzic is referring to when he put it to Mr. Nikolic that he had said on this page that civilians weren't targeted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was that interview and that page was added, but in that interview you said that legitimate military targets were concerned, and that is my question. Were these targets legitimate military targets? And the second question will be whether this is your conclusion or did you see an order according to which there were these targets?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to your first question is yes, but your question is very general, so I'll answer the question such as it is. Yes, legitimate military targets were targeted as part of the operation and attack on Srebrenica. And secondly, yes, legitimate targets were targeted in the town of Srebrenica during the operation to take Srebrenica until it was taken. I'm only speaking about my brigade's artillery battery now because I have information about that unit and I know that that unit fired on Srebrenica and fired on military targets located within Srebrenica. So that is one part of my answer. And now for the second part. You asked me about civilians and whether civilians were targeted, and I specifically said that, yes, during that period of time that was the case on the 11th in the evening when civilians were moving in the direction of Bratunac -- or, rather, in the direction of Potocari - I do apologise - I know for certain that from the position of the 2nd Infantry Battalion, civilians who were on the move were targeted. I -- I verified this, and I did have information. I was in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Infantry Battalion at that period of time. And when you asked who was targeted and why, when we saw that there were large masses of civilians who were arriving, well, they told me that they thought that these were military targets, which is why they fired on them with a B1 gun, that subsequently there was confirmation from the DutchBat representative and he told me that civilians in that area were targeted. So that concerns the targets along the axis of movement. As for the civilian victims in Srebrenica, I spoke about them yesterday. Yes, military targets were fired on, but, yesterday -- but a while ago I told you about what Srebrenica looked like. Quite frequently, and during that period of time, there were victims of artillery fire in Srebrenica who were civilians, and I have made that claim and I think that I have testified to that effect in all the cases and I'm confirming that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you have any information about civilian targets in that operation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to object and I'm not trying to break this up, but it just took me a moment to find it. I have one other clarification for the record. On page 34 at line 4, Mr. Karadzic asked the witness, Mr. Nikolic: "Is it correct that you had some knowledge then and other things you learned later, for example, concerning the participation of the army -- or, rather, the police, the MUP? You found out about that from what the OTP showed to you," and then he referred to the 4th of July information report on page 1. The only reference I find there to the MUP and finding out is bullet point 3: "Nikolic only found out about the letter from Minister Kovac, which refers to the Serbian police in Republika Srpska, RS, when the letter was disclosed by the OTP as part of the case against Blagojevic et al." Is that what Mr. Karadzic was referring to when he said that the witness only found out about the participation of the MUP, this letter about Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Robinson, I do not understand why Mr. Karadzic should rely on previous statements when he puts a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've explained that to him several times, to just put the question without reference to the statement. If the answer is inconsistent, to then put the statement, but he's having trouble doing that, but that's been my advice to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'm not objecting. I'm asking for some precision, because what's put to the witness is not always what is reflected in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: For Dr. Karadzic's benefit, if you don't reference a prior statement or testimony, then you don't have to make that kind of precision, which makes it much easier for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm talking about instances where it is referenced and it's not accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. I only wanted to have the witness assist us with regard to what he knew at the time and what he subsequently found out about, but I'll withdraw that. I won't go back to previous material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that -- or in fact, what was your hierarchical relationship to Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic and Kosoric? I don't know what his rank was. Were you their subordinate or were you only Colonel Blagojevic's subordinate?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that when I was examined by the gentleman from the Prosecution. As the intelligence and security organ, in command terms I was subordinated to my commander, the commander of the brigade, Colonel Blagojevic. But in professional terms, I was also the subordinate of Vujadin Popovic, the Department for Intelligence and Security in the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So your orders arrived from Colonel Blagojevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have my tasks in mind, not orders. My tasks on the whole were issued by my commander who exercised his command over me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you issue orders or assign tasks to a formation of some kind or to a unit? Did you exercise your authority in this command capacity?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a very general question yet again. I and no one from the intelligence or security field had a command function to exercise. We couldn't issue orders in our unit, nor could we issue orders to other units present in the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I have to go back to the meetings that were held. You spoke about a meeting held on the 11th of July, and you said that at that meeting you didn't hear anyone state clearly or explicitly that these people would be killed, but you had the feeling that that would happen. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say what you have just quoted. I wasn't at that meeting on the 12th. The meeting on the 12th took place at 10.00. I wasn't at that meeting, so I couldn't have said anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the transcript from the Popovic case, 33329 is the page reference, you said that you didn't hear such vocabulary being used on the 12th at that meeting. Now, could you now help us and tell us which meeting you did, in fact, attend?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended two meetings that were held in the Fontana Hotel. If we have the same meetings in mind, then we're talking about two meetings. One was held on the 11th in the evening. About 2000 hours was the first meeting, and the next one was held at 2200 hours, and at those two meetings I was present. This was in the Fontana Hotel. That's where the two meetings were held. And yesterday and over the course of the previous days, I said that I didn't participate in the meetings and I wasn't a representative of the Serbian side at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did General Mladic use the same words at that meeting as the words that were recorded by the camera which are in the transcript? Can we take that to be correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. All I can say is what was recorded there. I can't remember all the details. In general terms I know what happened at both meetings. I heard what was discussed, but I'm not a computer. I can't scan those things and reproduce them, but if you refresh my memory -- in any event, my answer is that what happened there, well, most of that conversation was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you personally ever have certain thoughts or intentions? Did you have the intention of driving away the Muslims from Podrinje or having them killed? Did any such thoughts ever occur to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a speculative question, and I personally wouldn't want to answer in a manipulative way. In the course of my life and work in the town of Bratunac, which is where I lived, such an idea never crossed my mind, because I was on exceptionally good terms with those people. I'm talking about my personal approach. I had friends among those people whom I would see. We would visit each other. So I personally never had any -- had any ill intentions towards those people, and I didn't make any distinctions between whether these people were Muslims or Serbs. I didn't have such a problem. And there is one other thing I would like to say. During that period before the war and in the course of the war itself, but before the war I wasn't a member of any political party, so I observed the political engagement of others from the side. So I had no reason to object to them for that reason too. In the part of town where I was born, I was trusted by Muslims and Serbs alike, and my position and the position of my family was sufficiently good. I had a sufficient amount of authority too. So I had absolutely no need to act in this way, and there's not a single Muslim who will tell you that Momir Nikolic was someone who bothered them or attacked them or insulted them, humiliated them, and so on and so forth, and this is a claim that I can categorically make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you the following: You were informed about this meeting on the 12th of July. That was the next day after those two meetings had been held. And with regard to that, you said that there was a visit to the bricks factory, and in the Popovic case, page 32904, you said that killing wasn't a subject that was explicitly mentioned at the meeting. Were you at that meeting with the director of the bricks factory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Karadzic? Just ask one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, is it correct that Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic and Kosoric told you about the meetings concerning the captured Muslims and locations in Bratunac, and were the Sase mine and the brickworks mentioned? And is it also correct that, as you claim, there were no killings discussed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you put a series of assertions that are incorrect. I have to say that. The first assertion you put was that as regards the meeting, I received some information or something to that effect. After the third -- sorry, the second meeting in the evening on the 11th, I knew. So no one told me anything or conveyed an order to me or issued a task to me for the next day. After the second meeting was over, General Mladic said that a meeting should be called at 10.00 the next day in the same place, the Fontana Hotel. So I heard it directly from General Mladic about the time and venue. Then he ordered me to escort DutchBat representatives and the Muslim representatives to Potocari. That was the first thing I wanted to say precisely. The next thing you said which was not correct was that there was a meeting at the brickworks, and you asked me whether I attended it. I have never thus far mentioned any meeting at the brickworks. I discussed a meeting, an encounter before the third meeting of Popovic, Kosoric, and myself, before the meeting on the 12th of July at 10.00 began at the Fontana Hotel. The next assertion which was incorrect was when you said that I attended that meeting. On the -- at the meeting on the 12th at 10.00, as I said during examination-in-chief, I was not present. I was not in the conference room. I did not hear what was discussed, and since I wasn't present, I didn't know what they decided. Throughout the meeting on the 12th at 10.00 at the Fontana Hotel, I was at the reception desk, which is a few rooms away. So there was no physical contact with the conference hall. I also spent some time outside in front of the Fontana Hotel where I kept an eye on the security measures in place in order to provide security for the participants of the meeting. Those are the facts in an attempt to tell the truth about what happened, where, and when. You asked about the brickworks --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. It was on the 14th. So I rushed ahead a bit.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I apologise. I'll wait for your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So at around 9.00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
