utterances.text: One, I don't like the witness being interrupted when what he's explaining are the incorrect assertions made. Second, just for the record, again at page 44, line 19, I won't go into it, but the reference to page 32904 is completely off base to what's reflected in the Popovic case. That concerns whether he had a discussion with Dusko Jevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Have a serious consultation with Mr. Robinson after this. I am really concerned about your ability to represent yourself in the interest of a fair trial for you, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I respect any opinion of the Chamber, but I am under a lot of stress because of the time pressure. I prepared to examine for nine hours, and I don't know what to discard now and still have -- receive a testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In any case, is it correct that your encounter with Kosoric and Popovic around 9.00 before the meeting, was not a meeting per se but a street encounter? So it wasn't a meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part of your assertion is correct. It was not an official meeting. The second part of your assertion is incorrect. It was an encounter in front of the Fontana Hotel, and it wasn't at around 9.00 but at around 10.00, just immediately before the third meeting on the 12th began.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you said that during the encounter, there was no mention of any killings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimony yesterday, I said precisely how the encounter developed. Mr. Popovic's statement that all Balijas should be killed is something I interpreted in my own way, and I've explained it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the extent of your knowledge or any documents you may have about those separated at Potocari? Did you refer to a specific number of the able-bodied men separated in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards those separated in Potocari and the number of men, I referred to two figures. The first was my assessment of how many people there were there. They were based on my own assessment and the assessment of my subordinate intelligence organs. The figure in question was between 1- and 2.000. And in my testimony, I have also referred to an approximate number of those who were separated on both days, the 12th and the 13th, during the evacuation. That figure is between 600 and 700 in the two days. So between 300 and 350 or 400 on the first day and on the second day. The number I mentioned, which I believe is highly likely, is between 600 and 700 of the people separated in Bratunac and the Vuk Karadzic school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You attended a meeting -- before that, on the 13th, you were in an APC with a policeman from which the Muslims were -- were called out to surrender by loudspeaker.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 13th. Well, for the benefit of the Chamber, I need to say that I was there twice, once in a passenger car, and on the next day, on the 13th, in the afternoon, I was together with Mirko Jankovic and Mile Petkovic, so the MP commander and his deputy, along the route Bratunac-Konjevic Polje-Sandici in an APC belonging to DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second Mr. Karadzic. I want to clarify your previous answer. I'll read out two sentences. First is this: "The first was my assessment of how many people there were there. They were based on my own assessment and the assessment of my subordinate intelligence organs. The figure in question was between 1- and 2.000." And later you said: "That figure is between 6 and 700 in the two days," meaning 12th and 13th. "So between 300 and 350 or 400 on the second day. The number I mentioned, which I believe is highly likely, is between 600 and 700 of the people separated in Bratunac and the Vuk Karadzic school." Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So first question is: 1- and 2.000, what do you refer to when you say there were 1- and 2.000 -- between 1- and 2.000 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I had in mind was my assessment about the number of men fit for military service who could be found in Potocari or would be found in Potocari after the arrival of civilians. I had in mind the men fit for military service as part of the large group of 30.000 people in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I understand. With respect to the second sentence I read to you, you said 6- and 700 people separated in Bratunac and the Vuk Karadzic school. Do you mean they were separated in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I was slightly confused. The people separated in Potocari, and they were less than our assessment. The figure is the amount of people who were separated in Potocari and then transported from Potocari to the detention facilities in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. This was useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you moved along that road, inviting the people to surrender, you didn't know what was in store for them, did you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th when I moved along that road, if you want to know about my feelings and beliefs at the time, then, of course, I didn't know and I wasn't 100 per cent sure, but I could sense something. It was my assessment that something bad would happen to those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So your feel of the situation was one thing, but if you knew for certain what would happen, you wouldn't have called them out, would you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't the person calling them out. It was Mile Petrovic. Now, as for whether I would call them to surrender, well, I think that if I knew a person would be killed, I wouldn't call anyone out. I think that question is something I have no answer to, but, yeah, I can definitely say that, personally, I wouldn't call out anyone if I were certain that they would be killed or liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that the reason why you were surprised when one of your colleagues told you that he had avenged his brother? You were told that by someone after you called out the Muslims and when some six Muslims were put in your APC. You heard some gunfire, and then you encountered a man who told you he avenged his brother; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was surprised by his act. I really didn't know then, and I still don't, whether his brother had been killed or not. In any case, individual acts of vengeance is something that happened there. 1994 and 1995 were the years of war, and nothing much surprised me then. I knew of many such actions on both sides. In any case, I was taken aback by what Mile Petrovic did, because I had believed he was a good policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Petrovic stated he didn't kill anyone and that it was some sort of rhetoric of his. Well, that's my interpretation, but do you know that he denied having killed anyone?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that Mile Petrovic denied it, denied the act of killing, but as for the rest, the entire event I put to you here is something he didn't dispute. To tell you the truth, I didn't even expect Mile Petrovic, or anyone else for that matter, who took part in the commission of any crime as part of revenge to confess, to come here and say, "Yes, I killed the six people because I wanted to get revenge for my brother." I never expected him to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you saw neither the killings or -- that killing or any other killing with your own pair of eyes.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all my testimonies so far, I said I did not see Mile Petrovic killing them. I didn't check the accuracy or truthfulness of his statement, and I also stated I have never attended or been present at any killing. I never saw anyone in person killing someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On your way back in the area of Sandici, on Sandici meadow you saw a group of prisoners. In your view, how many were there, and was it at around 2.00 or 3.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went through Sandici twice, both times in the afternoon. The first time I went by there were a few prisoners, not many. I don't want to guess, but not many. The next time it was later in the afternoon, between 4.00 and 5.00 or so, and by that time, they were people all along the road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje, and at Sandici there were many prisoners. I saw columns along the road of 2- to 300 people each. These are all my assessments, but there were many prisoners along the route. Some were moving towards Konjevic Polje, others towards Sandici and Kravica from Pervani, Lolici and Sandici. It is all something I saw myself on both occasions. The second time around, later in the afternoon, it was en masse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this figure you mention is between 200 and 300 if we take away the number of people en route to Konjevic Polje. So at Sandici how many were left, 150, 200? On the meadow itself.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again you have misquoted me. You are not presenting what I said correctly. I gave you an example. I saw one column at one spot that consisted of 250 to 300 persons, and I saw countless number of such columns. Well, not that big. That was a very big column. But I saw a countless number of other groups that were moving towards Konjevic Polje, in that direction, or towards Sandici and Kravica, the other way. I'm not talking about a single group. I'm talking about several groups. I'm talking about several people who had surrendered along the road that is about 10 kilometres long. From Kravica -- or, rather, Sandici to Konjevic Polje is about 10 kilometres. Along that road, people who had surrendered were moving along. There were groups that were moving on their own, without anyone escorting them or anyone having taken them prisoner. They were moving on their own, and I encountered them. There were columns where, for example, there was this big group that had been taken prisoner by the police who were there, and I saw that with my very own eyes. They were frisking them, probably for security reasons, reasons of their own, because there was also gunfire as they were surrendering. They would -- I mean, the man who would surrender would take out his pistol and shoot the policeman who was there. So then they were frisking people because that's what they should do, and I'm talking about these bigger groups of people. And I'm also saying that later on, when I came to Sandici, on the left-hand side, on a meadow, there was already a large number of people who were prisoners. I cannot tell you how many there were, but it was a large number. That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This large column was moving in which direction, Konjevic Polje or Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I passed by that column, they were standing on the right-hand side of the road towards Kravica, facing the middle of the road, and they were being checked by the members of the unit that had taken them prisoner. They were frisking them there. That is the biggest group that I saw. I don't know -- I mean, I passed by them in this APC. I don't know whether they went to Konjevic Polje or Kravica. That I do not know. I do not know where that specific group went.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on you say that during the day of the 13th, prisoners were coming in, people who had been taken prisoner in neighbouring municipalities, right, Milici and so on, and that large number of prisoners were flowing in. And you say that this was a major burden for Bratunac in terms of the security and safety of the city, or town.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one fact. Let us be very specific. I never said that people came from Milici. I said the prisoners were brought in from Nova Kasaba. Just to be very specific on that, Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, and it was from that direction that for the most part they were arriving nonstop, buses with persons who had been taken prisoner. Muslims who had been captured along that route or had surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is Nova Kasaba part of Milici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Previously I've been standing up asking for cites and not objecting. I am now objecting to Mr. Karadzic misstating to the witness what he allegedly said before. I object to putting to the witness that he has said things without any proper cites and which the witness says he has not said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. Nicholls. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, it's pretty clear what's going on. He's making misstatements and just hoping one will get adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for this imprecision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I mistaken in saying that Nova Kasaba is part of the municipality of Milici, or is it also part of the municipality of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you did not make a mistake. Nova Kasaba is a local commune in the municipality Milici. However, I just wanted to be precise because, according to my information, there were prisoners in Milici and in other places in the Milici municipality. I just wanted to state precisely what it was that I knew, and that is that from Nova Kasaba, prisoners were arriving in the territory of the municipality of Bratunac and they were being put up at facilities that were intended for detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that this was a major burden for you, especially as a security officer, and for the town itself?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a major problem for all of us who were there, regardless of whether we were soldiers or policemen or the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 13th, in the evening, was a meeting held that you attended as well? Can you tell us about that briefly, and can you tell us who attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I spoke about that meeting. That is to say, sometime after I returned from Zvornik, around 2400 hours, that is to say, around midnight, a meeting was held on the SDS premises, and I told you that the direct participants of the meeting were Miroslav Deronjic, president of the SDS; Colonel Dragomir Vasic, chief of the public security centre of Zvornik; and Colonel Beara, chief of the security administration of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were in the room itself, were you a participant in this meeting, or did you overhear it from an adjacent room?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not a participant in the meeting. I was sitting there in this reception area in the SDS offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For a while they were shouting. Did you hear any conversations that did not involve shouting? Did you miss anything?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I missed I could not have spoken about or testified about. I only testified about what I heard. I don't know. I think that I heard the essence of their conversation. Of course, again I would like to be very specific. I did not quote anyone. I explained in my own words how I understood their conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And there was this quarrel there when Beara and Deronjic referred to their bosses, mentioned their bosses; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were any of them under the influence even before they got out the drinks and glasses? Were they under the influence when the meeting started?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't analyse them then, but I said in one of my testimonies that one of them, that is to say, Colonel Beara, when he arrived to attend the meeting he was tipsy. That was my assessment. I may have been wrong, but I don't think I was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us the following now: Actually, you told us what your understanding was. Can you tell us now what words the two of them used as you remember them, or do we have to rely on that interpretation after these 17 years?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that question for you in part. I never said that I quoted them directly. I told you a moment ago that I told this Trial Chamber and every other time when I testified, I said what it was that I remembered or how I understood their conversation, and that is the conversation and content and those words that I testified about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 13th, after you returned from Zvornik, you also found out that there had been killings in Kravica. Is it correct that you were informed that this happened after the incident when a policeman was killed when a rifle was grabbed? Is that the information that you received as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about an incident in Kravica. I had that information that there were mass killings that were committed in Kravica, but that evening I was not aware of any details. A day or perhaps two days later, I knew a bit more about that, what it was that had really happened. And after I received an order from the command of the Drina Corps to investigate basically two questions, first, what was the structure that took part in the killings in Kravica, and -- actually, they knew roughly who it was, and I was supposed to investigate whether there were members of the military involved too. So I investigated that and I roughly confirmed what it was that I had known all along, that it was the police that had taken part, that a rifle was grabbed, that a policeman was killed, and after that these people were killed, liquidated, at Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that the Drina Corps command knew less than you did and that they sought information from you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that it was a question of who knew more and who knew less. Probably - again this is my assessment - they wanted to have an official confirmation of the information that they probably had available. They wanted to know who committed the killing, and they wanted a bit more detail. That's probably the only reason. For the command of the Drina Corps not to know, not to have information that a mass killing had been committed in their area, I mean, that kind of assertion -- well, you're not asserting that, but that kind of assertion I would find hard to believe now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, afterwards, someone decided that these victims should be buried in Kravica; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know where they were buried and whether they were buried in the same place or near to the location where the victims from May 1992 were buried, the operation of disarming Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know exactly where they were buried, those who got killed in 1992, and I know exactly where those who were killed in 1995 were buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh. Is that nearby?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the rest, who lost their lives elsewhere in Potocari, the school, or were killed at the school? They were also buried in Glogova, within this compound where those from Kravica had been buried as well; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will tell me who you're referring to from Potocari and which period you're referring to, I can give you an answer, because now I don't know who it is that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that there were five or six dead, that there was one suicide, and that a few persons were killed in different places, one, two, three in Srebrenica itself, and in Potocari itself there happened to be five to seven corpses that were buried in Glogova. It was the civilian protection that buried them in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any information -- actually, I never did have any information of a single killing in Potocari or of a group of people consisting of five or six or seven persons. The first and only time I heard of such information was when I read it in one of the statements given by one of the Dutch soldiers, but I was not aware of any killings in Potocari when all of those people were there during those critical days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps I misspoke. That is the number of corpses that was gathered there from different places, but, all right, if you're not familiar with this topic, we'll leave that. At the school there were what, 30, 50 dead? Do you know that they were also buried in Kravica -- actually, Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about my subsequent knowledge in relation to the killings that were committed in the hangar. That is in the immediate vicinity of the school that you referred to. However, what I know, that is to say, the information conveyed to me by Dragan Mirkovic who took part in cleaning up the area and in the burials, according to his statement these people were not buried in the same grave. Rather, they were transported to the village of Halilovici in the area of Glogova. I'm just conveying what I heard from him. And he said that they were buried there -- or, rather, that they were left there and, later on, that they were covered with earth. That is the information that I received from Dragan Mirkovic, who was commander of that unit for burials and for clearing the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was any conclusion reached at the meeting of the 13th? Was any decision taken at this meeting held on the 13th that you managed to hear from the adjacent room in the SDS premises, Beara, Deronjic, and others? Was any decision made?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting, a series of conclusions were adopted, and they were binding for the civilian police, the military police, the members of the military, and so on, and they had to do with securing those captives who had come from Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba and who were on buses. Also, there were conclusions and obligations that pertained to those who had been there from the 12th of July, that is to say, the 12th and the 13th. And finally, I spoke about this information and this quarrel, and finally they agreed that all the prisoners on the next day, 13th -- no, sorry, the 14th in the morning, should be transferred to the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, on the 14th in the morning, there was an attempt, was there not, to put them up in the brickworks? Did you visit the director of the brickworks together with Beara and these people?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went to the brickworks during that period. After the 13th in the evening, I never saw Colonel Beara again, nor did I contact him. On the 13th I saw him, on one day, the first time he issued an order to me, and the next time I saw him was when I took him to the SDS premises. And after that I didn't see Colonel Beara, and I didn't visit together with Colonel Beara or with anyone else the brickworks, the social brickworks company in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Beara went to see the director, and did you know what his intentions were when he went to visit the director of the brickworks?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've testified about that here. There was information according to which certain officers that -- I never said that it was Colonel Beara. I don't know about that. But I did testify here, and I'm repeating this, that I subsequently obtained information -- after all the events that unfolded there, I obtained information according to which a group of officers, I don't know who, really went to the brickworks, and they had contact with the director of the brickworks. They spoke to him about the killing of the captives who were in Bratunac. So that is the information that I subsequently obtained with regard to the visit made by some of the officers to the brickworks. But I don't know. What I heard was that they were there before the 13th, maybe even on the 12th, that would be the earliest date, but that is what I heard, and I wouldn't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time you did not know that they were looking for an execution site. That is something that in a certain sense was unveiled later, after the events. So now I want to find out what you knew at the time, what you found out at the time and what you found out at a subsequent date.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I didn't know that they went there, then naturally I couldn't know about their plans or about what they did. But I have to tell you this, and this is something I told you when we had our interview: The first time that it was discussed openly, it was no longer a secret, codes were no longer used, the first time that the fate of the soldiers was discussed, the first time that they openly discussed the killing of these people on the 13th in the evening, Miroslav Deronjic said this, roughly speaking, he said that he wouldn't want those people to be killed in Bratunac. He wouldn't allow it. He had enough problems. He insisted on them leaving the territory of Bratunac municipality. So that quite clearly showed that the fate of those captives was clear. It was clear that they would be killed. The question was whether they would be killed in Bratunac or whether they would be killed somewhere else, in this case in Zvornik. So that is what was quite clear at the time. There was no more dilemma as to whether they would be killed or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have two statements here from the director, Nedjo Nikolic, the brickworks director. He gave one to the Blagojevic Defence, and he gave the other one -- he sent it to us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D1508, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. The Chamber needs to rise for the moment. We will take a break now. We will take a break for an hour and resume at 1.20. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.20 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I won't waste any more time on these statements made by Mr. Nedjo Nikolic, but briefly assist us and tell us what sort of infrastructure the brickworks has in Bratunac. In addition to the administrative building, is there some sort of a room for drying bricks or for producing them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the infrastructure of the brickworks. I know that they were involved in producing these blocks and bricks. I know where the administrative building is, I know where they're located, where the factory is, but I really don't know much or anything about the infrastructure itself. They produced bricks and blocks of brick. That was their main activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "factory," does that mean that they had some sort of covered facilities, halls, rooms?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did have premises where they worked, and as far as I can remember, there was a place where they would work, and afterwards they'd take these things outside. They had a huge place where they could keep these bricks and blocks, where they could store them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to ask you the following: What made you take it upon yourself to admit certain things, to assume a significant amount of responsibility for certain things that you obviously did not do when you were trying to reach an agreement with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer your question in two parts. As for the first part, well, I have explained that in the course of my testimony. If you need additional explanations, I will provide them. As far as my admission of guilt is concerned and the written statement I gave, I will provide you with the explanations, but why did I admit I was guilty --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, there is no statement, just your testimony. I'm not asking why you admitted that you were guilty. Why did you admit that you had done certain things that you hadn't done? For example, at one point in time you were ready to assume responsibility. You said that you accepted that you were in Kravica in that company warehouse, and you said that you had ordered certain things. That was corrected later, but why would you admit that you had done something that you hadn't, in fact, done?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already explained the situation I was in to you at the time. I've also told you about the time when this arrived, and I explained something about the reasons for which I acted in this way. I don't have a particular explanation for why that is what I said. I naturally shouldn't have said anything of that kind. I quite simply wasn't there and didn't do that. I provided all the explanations for the reasons, but an additional reason would be that it was the end of the negotiations. I said everything I had to say. My lawyers had shown all the evidence I had to the Prosecution. They had handed all this evidence over to the OTP. So quite simply, to be frank, I was in a situation in which we had this agreement we'd been working on for a long time, and I didn't want it to fall through. I wanted this agreement to be reached. So I thought that if I entered the process, well, I should say everything that I had seen, everything I participated in. So apart from the reasons I've mentioned, that was an additional reason. Naturally, I understood that I had made a mistake. I accepted that kind of responsibility for -- because that's what I said. I admit that I made a mistake. It's easy to be a general after the fight, but the overall situation was such that this is something that happened. I'm just a simple man of flesh and blood. I accepted that. I made a mistake, I didn't tell the truth, I apologised, and then we continued with our work. That is my explanation. I have no other explanation to provide, and that is what I thought at the time and what I think now. I am being quite frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that you also accepted -- well, in fact, you falsely identified yourself. You said that man looked like you, but at some point you said you were quite desperate. You didn't want that agreement to fall through. You were ready to sacrifice yourself and to assume responsibility for something that you, in fact, had not done. Isn't that the case? And is there anything else that you accepted responsibility for?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the photograph is concerned, I also provided explanations for the photograph in the course of my testimony. If you like, I can tell you the reasons for the photograph now and at the time -- well, right now I didn't have the intention of placing myself somewhere where I wasn't present, but at the very beginning, the photograph that was shown to me and even a video, well, I analysed them countless times. The video -- in that video, the individual who appeared - and I think a photograph was made of that man - that individual really looked like me, so I thought that it was myself. When I was told it was in Sandici, that's the position was in Sandici, then I was in an even greater dilemma. I know that I was never in Sandici. I never got out of a vehicle or an APC in Sandici, but the photograph is from Sandici and then I told my Defence team that the photograph looks like me, the person in the photograph looks like me, the soldier in the uniform looks like me, or, rather, I look like him. However, given the place where the photograph was taken, as far as I know I never got out of the vehicle or an APC at that location. And then my Defence team carried out an investigation, looked into the entire matter and they established that it was Mile Savic in the photograph, also known as Cuko, from a MUP special brigade from Kozluk, and he worked on the border police. They took a statement from him, and then I was quite sure about the situation when he admitted that it was him. Then I was certain that I hadn't been there. I didn't want to be exclusive when speaking to the OTP. I didn't want to tell the Prosecution, "No, that's not me." How could I know? Perhaps I had forgotten something. Perhaps I couldn't remember something. So I didn't want to exclude the possibility. I said everything I have just told you. So that concerns the photograph. I really didn't have the intention now to make my situation even more difficult, but I just didn't want to exclude certain possibilities and deny something that had perhaps happened. That is my explanation and that is the only reason for which I made that admission. You also asked me whether there was anything else. In the statement that in some sense increased my responsibility, yes, there were certain phrases that didn't tally with each other, and initially I didn't pay much attention to these inconsistencies in the terms used. With time, I became convinced -- this just has to do with command and control elements, though. But with time, I became convinced of certain things. And I told my Defence team at an early stage, "Gentlemen, I don't think this can be attributed to me," and then they tried to persuade me of certain things. They told me how this didn't relate to certain matters. The concepts involved were concepts such as co-ordination. There were certain other concepts that I have listed and then corrected, but, really, when you read through it, this to a certain degree increases my responsibility. I wanted to be clear, and then in some later statement I tried to explain things as best I could. Without my Defence team, I tried to explain what I did there. I didn't change anything that concerned my participation, but I changed the phrases used. I eliminated certain terms that weren't appropriate to me but should be used in relation to the command. And in this manner, for the benefit of the Chamber and for everyone else, I tried to present a correct picture of the situation that I participated in. So when you take my factual basis, my conversation with the OTP, the statement given to them and the further statement provided, when you take all those elements into consideration and analyse them as a whole, then I'm convinced that to a great extent this reflects my participation, my responsibility, and my guilt in that operation, the operation that I participated in. So that is what I think I should say here in relation to all those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the OTP did not explicitly ask you to provide them with more information but it was your impression that the Prosecution wanted more information from you so that you could be sure that you would reach an agreement? You spoke about this in Blagojevic, page 2145. Did they ask for more information or were you guided by your impression of what it was necessary to do?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's neither one nor the other. I spoke to the OTP on countless occasions, and on countless occasions we addressed various issues, various subject matters. We spoke about everything that took place immediately before the operation, in the course of the operation, and after the operation in Srebrenica. I am from a field that fully understands the manner which an investigation is carried out. I know how you try to determine the truth. So the acts of the Prosecution were to a large extent correct. They insisted on establishing the truth. They wanted to determine what the truth was. Naturally, I could understand what their approach was. The OTP's task to establish the truth, and they have doubts about everything. So I had to be prepared for such a relationship and I was prepared. Of course, it's very difficult to go through all those things. It's very difficult and painful for everyone, including myself. It's difficult and painful to admit to facts that are not at all pleasant, that are extremely painful, extremely ugly, and it's stressful for everyone and for me, myself, to admit that you participated in something and to admit that you are responsible for something that can't be disputed, for a terrible crime. So in that sense, I fully understood the request that the Prosecution made. We spoke to each other on numerous occasions. We returned to certain issues. My only objection is now to my Defence team. It has to do with legal matters, and I as a layman didn't pay attention to that. I know about military things but not about legal matters. So as far as that that legal part is concerned from the agreement, the statement, my lawyers certainly knew what I participated in and what I did not participate in. So I was a hundred per cent frank with them. So here I have certain objections to make. When they were speaking to the Prosecution, why didn't the lawyers do everything that the lawyers should have done? So I have a serious objection to the way they proceeded. And because of their attitude, there were these problems that arose with regard to the definition of certain terms and the use of terms, and so on and so forth. So that would be my objection. But as for everything else, well, let me tell you, the negotiations were always difficult and stressful. Many things were repeated. The Prosecution insisted on addressing certain issues about which they had reliable information showing that they had happened and I participated in them or didn't participate in them, and this is how the overall negotiations were conducted. It was within that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see this agreement now. 65 ter 19459. If it shouldn't be broadcast -- well, could Mr. Nicholls please decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't see any reason it can't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We're coming up the agreement filed -- I see no reason that can't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm always in favour of having things out in the public domain. I believe this is a translation and the original should be English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your agreement, this agreement on the acceptance of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. This is a statement of facts and acceptance of responsibility, so it is a statement of facts and acceptance of responsibility. When I say "agreement," I mean something else. I mean another document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the agreement too. If this is authentic, can we please have the agreement admitted as well. We don't need to upload it. I mean, we don't have to display it if there is no dispute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just answer. As for the statement of facts and acceptance of responsibility, I made certain corrections in my secret statement and all the others are of a legal nature. My lawyers worked on that. I don't want to comment on that. I don't know how to comment on that, because the agreement basically refers to legal regulations. As for this statement, in addition to it, I submitted to the Trial Chamber certain matters that I tried to define more specifically, more clearly the role that I played and the roles that others played in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this part of the associated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that - I think it may be helpful - 65 ter 21586 is a supplemental statement which was prepared at the request of the Popovic Trial Chamber, which I believe is what Mr. Nikolic has been referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While we're trying to find our way through these documents, I would like to ask you something. You left the army without a rank; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the army with the rank of sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. When were you given this rank of captain?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got the rank of captain when I went to work in the Territorial Defence Staff, and then when according to establishment I met the requirements, I held a position that was that of an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have a degree in political science and you taught theory, so you were never prepared for a command role yourself or did you teach your pupils how to do that; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Command and control, that does not exist in secondary school. There is the subject called defence and protection, and it has a curriculum of its own. However, at the Faculty of Defence and Protection, I did have a subject called control and command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you did not have a unit that you could command; right? You did not have a unit that was under you? Is it correct that in your description you said that you prepared decisions related -- or, rather, recommendations related to the use of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All units including the military police in the Bratunac Brigade were directly commanded by the commander of the unit. I did not command it. I did not have a unit of my own, and that is not envisaged by establishment, not a single organ of this kind has his own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm even more surprised therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your time's up, so I would like you to conclude in five minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm even more surprised, then, because of this confession, because you did not have a unit under you. So tell us, who would be in charge of promoting you? If you were to be promoted, if you were supposed to be given a rank -- I mean, did you get a rank during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. During the war, I was a captain, and after the war I was promoted to the rank of major.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was in charge of your promotion? Was it the chain or was it the Bratunac Brigade, the commander of the brigade, or did it involve the professional chain, if you will?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All proposals for promotions to higher ranks and for citations and decorations are initiated by the commander of the basic unit that you're in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who made this proposal that you should be promoted to the rank of major? Who was commander then, or was it somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no proposal as far as my promotion to the rank of major was concerned. A law was passed then according to which all officers who held the rank of captain -- I mean, the next rank up the chain, captain first class was annulled. So if you held a particular position according to establishment and if you spent a certain amount of time in that position, three or four years, automatically you would be promoted to the next rank up. So in my case I was a captain, and I was promoted to the rank of major because the rank of captain first class no longer existed. Assistant commander for personnel affairs, Major Eskic, asked me to give him my booklet, and on the basis of the law, he wrote that in my booklet. He said rank of major. I don't remember the date but it was within my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell us when that happened? Could you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was just before my demobilisation, roughly. I don't know exactly. But at any rate, after the operation, after everything, and I think that it was all over, and I even think that the new commander had arrived. I don't know exactly. It is all in my military booklet and in my other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that was before the middle of 1996 or after that. When were you demobilised?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the exact date of my demobilisation is around the 20th of April, the 20th of April, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So when this proposal was made and when you were promoted, those who did that did not know anything bad about you; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained to you the way in which I was promoted to the rank of major. No one had anything bad to say, and I didn't have any recommendations either, and there were no evaluations made, good or bad. Major, Lieutenant-colonel, these were the further ranks. I held the rank of captain. I held a certain amount of time in that position according to establishment, so there was no need for anyone to make a proposal regarding myself. No disciplinary proceedings were ever instituted against me, so that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take a look at 1D5095?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So even in May UNPROFOR was treating you as a major, so obviously Serbs and foreigners thought that you should have more responsibility or, rather, that you held a position that was higher than what you actually held. It even says --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually can we have this document? Your Excellencies, actually this statement and the plea agreement, can that be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has it not been admitted, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. The plea agreement was admitted, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was -- what was that number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 21584 was the 65 ter number, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I don't remember the -- 4386, Your Honour. And I have no objection to the statement of facts and acceptance of responsibility being admitted provided that the direction or the additional statement is also admitted because it's clear that this one needed some correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the statement of the witness, we will admit both the statement of facts, this one, as well as supplemental statement, which was 65 ter number 21586.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits 2081 and 2082 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please take a brief look now at 1D5095.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this your last question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that is what it has to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I don't think that there's a Serbian translation. The 5th of May, 1995, a UNMO met with you and says that within the Army of Republika Srpska you are the liaison officer and more powerful than your rank suggests, and he considers you to be a major. And then he refers to Vukovic, that there was some protest that he had lodged. And then paragraph three -- [In English] I read it in English, sorry, to be translated better. [As read] "1. UNMO met Major Nikolic who is the BSA LO and rather more powerful than his rank suggests. "Given a letter of protest from Colonel Vukovic, commander of Skelani Brigade, and called liaison officer of Drina Corps for all matters concerning enclave. The letter was ref WF activities in the area. UNMO intend to reply on Monday. "BSA still awaiting a meeting with ABiH local joint commission, LJ, local joint commission will need discuss with the 2nd Corps at your level, will try to get copy of BSA proposal. "Comment: I believe BSA warned the LJC in order to withdraw troops from other areas. ABH aware of this and will keep stalling." [Interpretation] Further on, it says down there there's a comment: [In English] "Comment from team: Major Nikolic clearly trying to demonstrate BSA willingness to talk and discuss any violation within his own area of responsibility. BSA have even stated willingness to go anywhere in enclave for meeting with BiH, but so far, 28th Division have refused." [Interpretation] So the UN considers you to be a powerful officer and rather more powerful than your rank of major suggests. But then further down there are words of praise that you clearly demonstrated the readiness of the Army of Republika Srpska to discuss any violations. Was that the way it was? Did that happen in May 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 5th of May, 1995, and on any other date, whenever members of UNPROFOR asked to see me, I would go to see them, unless I was forbidden to do so. So there were periods when there was this ban on my meetings with him -- with them. The Dutch can confirm that I even entered Muslim-controlled territory in the area of Vresinje, in the area of responsibility of the 1st Infantry Battalion. I also entered Potocari several times and negotiated with them. Every time they asked for this I was there at their disposal, and I conveyed their requests to the superior command depending on the type of request involved. Sometimes to the Main Staff and always to the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nikolic, do you accept that all reports with your signature are your own and that I could submit them as bar table motions, because we don't have time to go through each and every one of them? Do you stand by all your reports? I don't know if the Trial Chamber will accept this, but in principle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, how can he answer the question without seeing them? Come to your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted as next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2083, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My last question for Mr. Nikolic. I'll try to put it in a summarised form and I'll ask you to try and answer in one go. Were you close with Popovic, Beara, Blagojevic, Kosoric and others? What was your relationship with them, whether they were your military colleagues or in the sphere of politics?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know I was not involved in politics, especially if you have in mind the highest political level. I was never a member of the SDS, and in that regard, I was not close to any -- with any politicians. I did have a good working relationship with the politicians in my municipality, and we never encountered any particular problems, but I did not socialise with them. We did not have that kind of relationship. We held each other in high professional regard, and we assisted each other as people do, but I had no friends in political circles. As for the officers you mentioned, I was not friends with any of them. I did not complete the military academy, and I had not worked in the JNA units they had. I heard for the first time of those people once they became part of the Drina Corps and Main Staff. I met with them officially on their request or on their orders or the orders of the superior command. My relationship with the officers you mentioned, starting with Mladic, Beara, Popovic, Kosoric and others, was a professional one and fair throughout the time. I never came into any conflict with any of them privately or professionally, and I always strove to carry out my duties as prescribed by the Law on the Military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you oppose today the events of 1995? Would you refuse to do what was asked of you back then if such actions were not part of the rules?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm 17 years older now. I'm not that much smarter, but at least I am more experienced. Mr. Karadzic, you learn from your life's problems, and you keep learning. Experience works miracles. If I were to be in -- in a similar situation knowing what I know now, trust me, I wouldn't be fooled by anyone. I wouldn't carry out anyone's order. I would simply flee if in the same situation. But then, things were completely different. The situation was different, and I carried out my superiors' orders, and by having done so I made mistakes. As a human being I accepted that, and I believe anyone in such a situation should. When things are fine and going well, one needs to accept the praise. In case of mistakes, one needs to take the blame, and I do to the extent of my guilt and the mistakes I made. I did that, and I feel no regret for having done that. I felt much relieved once I accepted my responsibility and said that I was sorry for what I had done. In a way, I feel better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you have any expectations on the part of the Prosecution to agree to you being released after having served two-thirds of your sentence, and do they have any expectations of you in the next case, the Mladic case, to testify again? I'd like to conclude with that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what the intentions of the Prosecution are. As any detainee, any inmate, I will always try to have my early release requests granted. I don't know what the decision would be, whether the President of the Tribunal would grant that or not, but I will make use of any rule under the Finnish law. The President of this Tribunal and its Judges will render their decision, and I will honour it no matter what it may be. As for the opinion of the Prosecution, I don't know what it will be. Within the existing procedure, they need to provide their opinion on my behaviour and possibility of my return to the society as someone who had participated in it all. It is up to them, not up to me. But in any case, I will always invoke my right to submit my request for release to the President of this Tribunal. I believe that I am under an obligation to appear. Whether I was asked to do that by the Bench, the Prosecution, or a Defence, I have to come to testify as I did in the past proceedings and in the future proceeding of Mr. Mladic, if it should come to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I conclude my cross-examination earlier, because as I have said already, I had planned to use nine hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's unacceptable, Mr. Karadzic, for you to say so after having spent eight hours and 25 minutes. In any event, yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then unless my colleagues have questions for you, Mr. Nikolic, that concludes your evidence. Just before that, Mr. Nicholls, I need your guidance. Line 4 does not need a redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe there is no need, Your Honour. Could I have a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Yes. It's no problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Nikolic. On behalf of this Bench and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you sincerely for your coming to The Hague again. I wish you all the best.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am always at your disposal when needed to come and testify to the extent possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We do appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd also like to thank you, Ms. Lindsay. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: MS. LINDSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We just need a couple minutes, Your Honours, to change positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while they're changing positions, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: With respect to this next witness, there is going to come a point when his 92 ter statement is offered that we're going to object to a certain portion of that, and we could wait to -- that time, or we could deal with that issue before he comes in, whatever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we deal with it now, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. I will wait until they get settled and then I'll start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it would be better to be dealt with in his absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. This is a request that the Trial Chamber not admit the last sentence of paragraph 25 and paragraph 26 of the amalgamated statement of the next witness, journalist Robert Block, and that deals with the issue of his claim that Dr. Karadzic was very angry and demanded that the tape of Srebrenica footage be recovered. And it's our position that the information that Mr. Block has about that is insufficiently reliable to be admitted, so I would like to just briefly give you the facts of what we're dealing with and then explain a little about some jurisprudence that we're relying on. First of all, in the amalgamated statement, Mr. Block indicates that he got that information from two sources. His first source is his driver and interpreter who he refuses to identify. It's not identified in the amalgamated statement, and when we had our interview with him yesterday afternoon, he told us that he didn't want to identify that person. He also indicated and I believe he would also testify that that person had no access to Dr. Karadzic and was "doing the rounds in Pale," and that the person was essentially hearing rumours and that that was the source of his information about Dr. Karadzic's reaction. The second source for Mr. Block is a conversation he said that he had with the film-maker Goran Petrovic-Pirocanac in the presence of his, Mr. Block's friend and colleague Dragan Cicic, and according to Mr. Block, he said that Mr. Petrovic gave no indication as to where he had gotten the information about Dr. Karadzic's reaction, and as far as Mr. Block knows, Petrovic had not spoken with Dr. Karadzic directly. He told us he had the impression that perhaps one of Mr. Petrovic's friends had said to Mr. Petrovic that, Even Dr. Karadzic is upset with you. So the information that Mr. Block purports to give to the Trial Chamber is at least at a minimum triple hearsay. We start with Mr. Block. The first level of hearsay is what he's told either by his driver, who is anonymous, or Mr. Petrovic. The second level of information is someone who we don't know who told Mr. Petrovic or the driver. And the minimum third level of hearsay would be if Dr. Karadzic had told that person, and we don't even know if there are other intermediaries involved. So we believe that, for one, the circumstances show that this is not the kind of evidence that is reliable enough to be admitted in this Tribunal, even a Tribunal that admits hearsay evidence. And there are other circumstances that militate against the reliability of this hearsay information. Mr. Block wrote an article on the 21st of July, 1995, in which he wrote that the footage of the Srebrenica taken by Republika Srpska TV was confiscated under the orders of the Bosnian Serb Army, and that's 65 ter 21961. It's an associated exhibit. The person who accompanied him when he met Petrovic, Dragan Cicic, also wrote an article that same day, and he wrote that the footage was confiscated by military authorities and in the hands of the army of the Bosnian Serbs. So the contemporaneous reporting about what happened to this tape -- these tapes make no mention of Mr. Karadzic and indicate that it was the army who had acted. And Mr. Block has indicated to us that this was not -- Dr. Karadzic's reaction was not something that he tried to corroborate, that it was not relevant for his article, and he was simply reporting, and as long as the army had confiscated the tapes, that was all that mattered to him at the time. I note also that in an interview given by Mr. Cicic to the Prosecutor in 2009, he makes no mention whatsoever of any comment that Petrovic made referring to Dr. Karadzic, and, in fact, he indicates that Petrovic referred to the army when discussion the confiscation of the footage. And finally, Mr. Petrovic himself has been interviewed by the Prosecution, has testified in two trials, including the Popovic testimony which has been admitted under Rule 92 bis in this trial, and as far as I can tell, he's made no mention of having information that Dr. Karadzic had ordered the confiscation of the tape or had been angry about it. So that's the factual background. The legal aspect is this: That hearsay evidence is only admissible when the Trial Chamber is satisfied that the evidence is reliable, and the appeal -- that's from the Appeals Chamber, and that the reliability of a hearsay statement is relevant to its admissibility and not just its weight. Also Appeals Chamber decision in Kordic and Cerkez. And that since hearsay evidence once admitted constitutes substantive evidence, it's important that its reliability be established, and whether the hearsay is first-hand or removed is relevant to determine the probative value of the evidence. There's two decisions in the Milutinovic case where the Trial Chamber, led by Judge Bonomy, excluded evidence on hearsay grounds with principles that I think should be applicable here. In the first decision, which is decision on evidence tendered through Sandra Mitchell and Frederick Abrahams of the 1st of September, 2006, the Trial Chamber denied the admission of OSCE and Human Rights Watch reports which contained information gathered in the field by their personnel. And the Trial Chamber said essentially that this material which contained information based upon investigations conducted by these organisations were not sufficiently reliable to be admitted without the opportunity to have those statements tested through cross-examination of the declarants, and that the reports "As Seen, As Told" and another report about Kosovo events would not be admitted because the Chamber did not have before it sufficient material to satisfy it of the reliability of the underlying information upon which those reports were based. And in a subsequent decision, decision denying the Prosecution's motion for admission of evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis of the 13th of September, 2006, the Milutinovic Trial Chamber refused to admit a collection of what was called Kosovo Emergency Updates prepared by international humanitarian organisation which contained accounts of displaced persons, including the reasons why they were displaced. And the Trial Chamber said that, again, it didn't have a basis for assessing the reliability of the underlying statements, and the fact that the statements constituted second-hand or even more removed hearsay, seriously weakened whatever probative value they might otherwise possess. And finally, the Chamber went on to say that even if the documents were admissible, they would decline to admit the statements because fairness would require that those who made the accusations or who claim to have heard the accusations being made appear for cross-examination. So for all of those reasons, we believe that the information relayed by -- proposed to be relayed by Mr. Block is insufficiently reliable to be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The issue here essentially boils down to one thing and that is whether the evidence of Mr. Block has sufficient probative value and sufficient reliability to be admitted, and I'd submit that there are two reasons why this is sufficiently reliable and probative for admission in this case. The first is, and I would cite to the Aleksovski appeal decision of 16th of February, 1999, where the Appeals Chamber said that the admission of hearsay evidence or the reliability of hearsay evidence depends very much on the circumstances under which the evidence arose. And I'd submit that the circumstances under which Mr. Block heard this information clearly makes it probative and reliable for admission. He went on the 17th of July, 1995, to Studio B to find that this footage had disappeared. The next day, he went to Zoran Petrovic's house to find out what had happened to this footage and heard directly from Zoran Petrovic that Dr. Karadzic had been very upset about it. That's a direct, reliable, probative statement of why this footage went missing. The second point I'd like to make is Mr. Block's evidence is at least consistent with or corroborated by two other pieces of information which are already in evidence in this case. The first is Dr. Karadzic's appointment diary for 1995 has at least two entries where Zoran Petrovic-Pirocanac has direct contact with the President. So we know that there is an existing relationship there. The second piece of consistent or corroborating evidence comes from a speech by Dr. Karadzic himself, which is in evidence as Exhibit P1412. It's a speech given by Dr. Karadzic at the 52nd Assembly Session on the 6th of August, 1995. And perhaps we could bring that up. It's page 75 in the English and page 64 in the B/C/S. And just to be clear, we're not saying that the footage that Dr. Karadzic is talking about in this speech is necessarily the exact same footage of Zoran Petrovic-Pirocanac, but it's directly corroborative of Dr. Karadzic's state of mind about or what he felt about this footage being in the public domain. It's page 75 in English. Dr. Karadzic says: "The cameras record everything that must not be recorded, after which they broadcast it and give it to foreign agencies. Lieutenant-Colonel Milutinovic has given information to foreign agencies. There is information that he has sold information. I do not care if he took 25.000 German marks or not, but he has given disastrous pictures to foreign agencies, pictures that could cost Mladic his life if they were presented in The Hague. They broadcast whatever they want, and they have recorded corpses of women in the streets of Srebrenica, after which they broadcast that on foreign media." So to sum up my position, the specific circumstances under which Mr. Block acquired this information is sufficiently -- gives it sufficient relevance and probative value to be admitted as well as the corroborating evidence that I've just referred you to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I respond to this, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This discussion involves the recalcitrance of a number of officers whom I do not hold as my officers. They were listed there, and it had nothing to do with Pirocanac. It had to do with Radio Krajina, who, in the middle of the war, functioned as an opposition to the government. So in other words, it amounted to the work carried out by a part of the military against the state. It involved the work of the press centre at Pale. It has nothing to do with Pirocanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, just very briefly. I'm not sure what the reference to Radio Krajina was, but Dr. Karadzic specifically referred to Srebrenica in that speech.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add something briefly. The main objection is to the selection of foreign press agencies rather than objectivity. They published and broadcast what they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the issue when and -- and issue the ruling next week. Unless there are any matters to deal with today. Yes, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness is here and ready to start if we're sitting till 3.00 today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then could you cover the issues that's not related to paragraph 25 and 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And do you have any objection to that step, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your suggestion. Please bring in the witness. Mr. Mitchell -- yes, Mr. Nicholls --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. It just occurs to me while we're talking, that it might be better, with half an hour left, I think, to get the ruling. Then it would be completely clear where we could go, where we couldn't. It won't trigger something that gets another objection or a statement. But the witness doesn't know yet what the ruling is, and it may make it smoother, and are we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That sounds simpler, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it viva voce or -- I wasn't sure what the ruling is on the -- or is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we'll -- whatever the ruling may be, we were minded to order the Prosecution to lead live what is contained in paragraphs 25 and 26. That said, the witness will be admitted as Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then do you suggest adjourning for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Who will explain to the witness? I will leave it to the Registrar. Then let him in then -- okay. Thank you. Then we will resume next week, Tuesday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
